OwnableInvalidOwner(address).details: The owner is not a valid owner account. (eg. `address(0)`)

OwnableUnauthorizedAccount(address).details: The caller account is not authorized to perform an operation.

SafeERC20FailedOperation(address).details: An operation with an ERC-20 token failed.

claim().details: Safe, and deliberately pointless, to call when you have won nothing: it transfers an         encrypted zero and costs gas. That is the design. If claiming only worked for         winners, then calling it would announce that you are one.

fundReserve(uint64).details: This is the mock yield source, and it is deliberately the least clever thing here.         A testnet produces no real yield, so prizes are funded directly, and the amount is         public so that anyone can check the pool is able to pay what it advertises.         A production deployment replaces this one function and nothing else: principal goes         into a lending venue and the surplus over principal becomes the reserve. Worth         stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered, that step would make the         aggregate amount deployed visible to that venue. Individual balances would stay         encrypted; the pool's total would not.

onConfidentialTransferReceived(address,a.details: This is the entire deposit path. A depositor calls `confidentialTransferAndCall` on         the token and lands here, so depositing costs one transaction and needs no prior         approval of the pool at all. The only approval anywhere in the journey is the         ordinary ERC-20 one needed to wrap plain tokens into confidential ones.         `amount` is what the token actually moved, not what the sender asked it to move.         ERC-7984 transfers do not revert on an insufficient balance, they move zero and         return a handle saying so, and crediting the request rather than the movement would         mint principal the pool never received.

openDraw().details: Permissionless, because there is nothing to gain by calling it. The caller cannot see         the result any more than anyone else can.         The winning point must land uniformly inside the pool's total, and that total is         encrypted. Remainder accepts only a plaintext divisor, so `random % total` would         force the total into the clear, and a public total lets anyone recover individual         deposits by subtracting one draw's total from the next. Widening both sides to 128         bits, multiplying, and shifting back down by 64 produces the same uniform result with         the total still sealed. The only bias is in the discarded low bits, on the order of         one part in 2^64.

owner().details: Returns the address of the current owner.

renounceOwnership().details: Leaves the contract without owner. It will not be possible to call `onlyOwner` functions. Can only be called by the current owner. NOTE: Renouncing ownership will leave the contract without an owner, thereby disabling any functionality that is only available to the owner.

scanChunk(uint256).details: Permissionless and resumable. It is split across transactions because the running         total is a chain of dependent encrypted additions, and the coprocessor caps how deep         a single transaction is allowed to go.         Every depositor is written, winner or not, and every write costs the same. A scan         that skipped the losers would identify the winner by which storage slot changed.

transferOwnership(address).details: Transfers ownership of the contract to a new account (`newOwner`). Can only be called by the current owner.

withdraw(bytes32,bytes).details: The request is clamped to the balance rather than checked against it. A check would         mean branching on an encrypted comparison, which cannot be done, and reverting on         "too much" would leak the balance to anyone patient enough to binary search it.

SenderNotAllowedToUseHandle(bytes32,addr.notice: Returned if the sender is not allowed to use the handle.

ZamaProtocolUnsupported().notice: Returned if the Zama protocol is not supported on the current chain

asset().notice: The confidential asset the pool holds. Every balance here is denominated in it.

claim().notice: Moves whatever the caller has won into their own wallet.

confidentialBalanceOf(address).notice: A depositor's principal, encrypted. Readable only by them, through EIP-712 user decryption.

confidentialWinningsOf(address).notice: A depositor's unclaimed winnings, encrypted. This is how a winner finds out they won.

fundReserve(uint64).notice: Adds plain tokens to the prize reserve, wrapping them into the confidential asset.

maxChunk().notice: The most depositors one transaction may scan. The scan is a chain of dependent encrypted additions, so it spends the coprocessor's per-transaction depth budget rather than its width budget, and the real ceiling is a property of the live network rather than of this code. This is set from measurement against the deployed coprocessor, which is why it is a variable and not a constant. Measured on Sepolia: 29 depositors are accepted and 30 are refused with `HCUTransactionDepthLimitExceeded`. That matches the cost tables exactly, at one dependent 64-bit addition per depositor (162,000) plus 223,000 for the trailing comparison and select, against a budget of 5,000,000. The default sits below the ceiling so that a coprocessor repricing does not turn every draw into a revert overnight.

nextDrawAt().notice: When the next draw may be opened. Zero means now.

onConfidentialTransferReceived(address,a.notice: Credits a confidential transfer sent directly to this pool.

openDraw().notice: Opens a draw and picks the hidden winning point.

prizePerDraw().notice: What the next draw pays out.

reserve().notice: Unspent prize funding, in token units. Public on purpose, so solvency can be checked.

scanChunk(uint256).notice: Walks the next `count` depositors of the draw in progress.

scanTransactionsRemaining().notice: How many scan transactions the draw in progress still needs at the current chunk size.

setMaxChunk(uint256).notice: Tuned from what the live coprocessor actually permits, which is why it is not a constant.

underlying().notice: The plain ERC-20 underneath it, used only to fund the prize reserve verifiably.

withdraw(bytes32,bytes).notice: Takes principal back out, in any amount, at any time, including mid-draw.

userdoc.notice: No-loss prize savings where every amount is encrypted end to end.         Deposit any amount of the confidential asset. Your principal stays yours and can be         withdrawn in full at any moment, including while a draw is running. At each draw the         prize reserve pays out to one depositor, chosen at random, with odds exactly         proportional to what they hold.         ## What is public and what is not         Public: the addresses that have ever deposited, the size of each jackpot, and when draws         happen. An address is public because a deposit is a transaction sent from one, and no         design choice here can change that.         Private: every individual balance, the pool's total, the winning ticket, who won, and how         much anyone has won. None of these is ever decrypted on chain, by anyone, including the         owner of this contract.         ## Why the draw cannot be rigged         The random value is generated inside the transaction and is never decrypted. Neither is         the winner. So whoever calls the draw cannot see its outcome, and therefore cannot throw         away an outcome they dislike and try again. The unpredictability is not a promise about         the caller's good behaviour, it is a consequence of them being unable to look.         ## How a winner is chosen without anyone learning who         Line the depositors up and lay their stakes end to end. The draw picks a hidden point on         that line, and whoever's stake covers it wins, which makes the odds proportional to stake         size by construction rather than by adjustment. Walking the line, a running total crosses         the hidden point exactly once, so a flag flipping from false to true marks the winner and         marks nobody else. The prize is then added to every depositor's winnings through that         flag: the real amount for one of them, zero for all the rest. On chain those writes are         indistinguishable from each other.         Each depositor decrypts their own winnings with an EIP-712 signature. The winner learns         they won because their number went up. Nobody else learns anything at all.
